extracted.intended_audience: NLP / multimodal AI researchers and developers working on humor understanding and captioning
extracted.subtask_description: Benchmarks and evaluation tasks derived from the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest for assessing model 'understanding' of humor, including matching captions to cartoons, selecting winning captions, and generating explanations of why captions are funny. Includes dataset annotation standards and evaluation protocols comparing multimodal and language-only models to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching a joke to a cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching a joke to a cartoon (one of three tasks derived from the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This task encapsulates sophisticated aspects of 'understanding' a cartoon, requiring models to handle the complex, often surprising relationships between images and captions. Performance is measured (e.g., accuracy); the paper reports best multimodal models fall ~30 accuracy points behind human performance on this task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying a winning caption
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying a winning caption (select which caption would win the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selection task tests a model's ability to judge caption quality in contest-style settings and captures higher-level, contest-relevant notions of funniness and appropriateness that go beyond literal image-caption fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explaining why a winning caption is funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate an explanation of why a winning caption is funny (the third, more sophisticated task).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations are evaluated via human preference head-to-head comparisons; even when provided ground-truth visual scene descriptors, human-authored explanations are preferred over best machine-authored ones (few-shot GPT-4) in more than two-thirds of cases. Task requires capturing indirect/playful allusions and connections to human experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal vs language-only evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare multimodal models (given cartoon images directly) with language-only models (given multifaceted textual descriptions of the visual scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language-only models are tested with rich scene descriptions to simulate human-level visual understanding. Benchmarks should explicitly evaluate both modalities to understand where visual grounding or textual scene description suffices or fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset annotations: locations/entities, unusual elements, explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus includes annotations describing the image’s locations/entities, what’s unusual in the scene, and an explanation of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These annotations serve as structured supervisory signals and evaluation inputs (e.g., for language-only models) and set a standard for dataset content required to probe image-caption relationships and humor reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics: accuracy and human preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quantitative accuracy for matching/selection tasks and human preference judgments for explanation quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported metrics include accuracy gaps to humans (example: ~30-point accuracy gap on matching) and human pairwise-preference rates (example: human explanations preferred >2/3 of the time versus machine explanations). Benchmarks should report both objective task accuracy and subjective human-evaluation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key challenge elements for humor understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful humor understanding must handle complex, often surprising relationships between images and captions and frequent inclusion of indirect and playful allusions to human experience and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark design and evaluation should emphasize these aspects (indirectness, cultural allusion, surprise, interplay between visual context and caption) because they are central challenges that cause models to struggle.
